title: Forgiveness and Accountability Go Hand-in-Hand
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece argues that forgiving mistakes quickly and holding people accountable for fixing them are complementary, not contradictory, leadership moves. It contrasts a punitive model — reprimanding people for errors, which teaches concealment — with a model where sanctions are reserved for those who hide mistakes, not those who own them. Under the recommended approach, once a mistake is forgiven, the person who made it (not the leader) is expected to propose the remedy, turning accountability into ownership of a solution rather than punishment for a failure. The piece frames this combination as treating mistakes as opportunities for development rather than occasions for blame.
points: The article distinguishes between reprimanding honest mistakes (which teaches concealment) and reserving sanctions only for those who cover mistakes up.
Accountability, in this model, means the person who erred proposes their own remedy — leaders forgive quickly but don't hand over the first solution.
The piece explicitly rejects the "leader as taskmaster" model of reward and punishment, calling it discredited as the primary mechanism for driving performance.
Forgiveness and accountability are framed as two complementary forces — one an attitude, one a discipline — that together turn failure into a developmental opportunity.
quotes: Sanctions and reprimands are reserved for those who cover up mistakes, not for those who acknowledge them.
Once forgiven, team members are held accountable in a way that motivates, rather than demoralizes, them.
Good leaders don’t offer the first solution or strategy to resolve or manage the situation. The person who made the mistake does.
In reality, penalizing people for anything other than a colossal mistake is a surefire way to destroy team morale and encourage people to cover up anything that goes wrong.
This also treats failures as an opportunity for learning and growth.
Forgiveness is an attitude. Accountability is a discipline. Marry the two together and leaders connect the past and the future in a way that compassionately develops people.
